t: How To Get Your Misbehaving Class Back On Track
q: When a class gets off track, the tendency is to talk. It’s to rehash, remind, and redo. It’s to circle-up the community, lecture and rebuke.
After all, they’ve just proven that they can’t handle the freedom within the boundaries you currently have. So you must adjust to match their needs.
It doesn’t matter what it is. But limiting existing freedoms, or otherwise requiring more discipline from your students, is the one thing guaranteed to get their attention.

Show fear in the face of losing control, become stressed and emotional, and behavior will get worse, not better. Calmly and confidently tighten your boundaries, however—even in just one little area—and they’ll give in. They’ll acquiesce.
Once you have control and impeccable behavior, proven over time, you can remove the new line. You can extend the boundary and allow more freedom and responsibility.

t: How To Shorten Your Work Day
q: Efficiency has been a priority for me for the past 31 years of teaching. It’s a big reason why I continue to teach, with zero plans to retire.
Former Navy Seal and author Jocko Willink has a book called Discipline Equals Freedom , and I think it’s absolutely true. To make room for life outside of school, you must have discipline.
Parkinson’s Law is the tendency for organizations and individuals to expand a task in complexity and importance in relation to the time given for its completion.
I recommend getting started by creating a firm time for leaving school that moderately challenges you to get your work done. When that no longer becomes a challenge, shrink the deadline.
You’re not moving faster per se, you’re getting smarter and more discerning, which translates to speed. You may even find yourself physically slowing down and becoming calmer .

t: End of Year Motivation Moves, Part 2 — Work the Roster
q: It's hard in a good way — for students you've had a hard time with, you'll have to take some time or a walk just to try to figure out what to say to them about what you've appreciated.
You know, there was a time this year when this kind of drove me crazy about you. Funny, right? But look: I think it's something special about you, this mind that wants to know how things work.
You've wrestled, haven't you? You've fought! There've been lots of times when you've told yourself — don't deny it, you said it right in front of me! — "I can't do this. I'm going to fail.
Early in the school year, I don't think we quite knew what to make of each other. Or, let me just speak for me — I didn't know what to make of you!
The person I see in front of me today is a different, deeper, stronger person than the one I met last September. Thanks for letting me in on a bit of your life story, Herbert.

t: Student Motivation at the End of the School Year
q: We can crawl across the finish line, counting down the seconds until it's summer break because we can't wait for a rest. OR we can march across the finish line, limping a bit from the hardships of these past years, heads held high, hearts full.

When folks are on the left side of the curve, like I was, the last thing they'll respond well to is someone offering a challenge; these folks are over-pressured already, and challenge is the language of pressure.

BUT, when folks are on the right side of the curve, then what they absolutely need to experience a performance enhancement IS a challenge! They are under-pressurized and, as a result, are probably experiencing boredom and ennui.
What if we made class into a chance to grow and be with people we like — not some dark place where we're constantly failing to prove our worth?
You're not differentiating the content students are learning or the assignments in your classroom so much as you're differentiating the ways in which you approach the hearts of your young people.

t: The First Step With An Out-Of-Control Class
q: With an out-of-control class, bringing up rules right away will fall on deaf ears. No, the first step after losing control or taking over an unruly class is to remove excitability .
The culture is broken and can only heal when restlessness, tension, and agitation are removed. Only then can you introduce your classroom management plan and get a handle on misbehavior.
It’s to become so calm yourself that your peaceful energy spreads to every student in the class. I know it sounds new-agey, but it’s effective.

By your presence alone you’re pulling your students into your corner, on your side, and within your sphere of influence. Your calm likability will give you just enough space to be heard and listened to.
Build connection. Establish likability. Bring in fresh oxygen, a new vibe, and a common, more peaceful wavelength. Breathe in and out. Smile.

t: Value Booster: Why Are You Here?
q: After answering several such questions, the research participants started to think about their goals either more abstractly [the WHY group] or more concretely [the HOW group] depending on the series of questions they'd answered. Those who answered a series of 'why' questions were more motivated to channel resources to their goals.
Telling someone that "I maintain good physical health so that I can be a more energetic father" does something to your heart that telling someone "I run three times per week" just doesn't do.

My take is that the WHY question format activates the Value belief in the hearts of participates. This kind of makes sense when you compare the Fujita experiment above with one I wrote about in These 6 Things.

The student-generated kind is, of course, the more resilient — this is why Hulleman's studies end up yielding results years after the intervention. When my students leave my classroom at the end of the year, I don't travel along on their shoulders, daily explaining the beauty of an education.
Your first goal? To listen and understand the hearts of the people you teach. Your second goal? Who knows — maybe they'll start holding the handgrip a little harder tomorrow.

t: Learning Lesson 8: It's Easy to Trick Yourself into Thinking You Know More Than You Know han-you-know
q: Folks are often OVERCONFIDENT when judging how well they understand something. Let's get that down.

One reason that's true is because those are passive strategies — they don't require much effort, and they don't really require you to understand anything. But another reason is that they make you overconfident.
The way to fix this overconfidence really quickly is to test yourself! All right — so, how can we test ourselves?
The only way to know if you know something is to test yourself. And what's cool is that the act of testing yourself is actually a good method for overlearning material and making it automatic.
There's no way to have an optimally motivated class of learners who have not had a chance to learn more about learning in that class. We gotta teach 'em how to advance toward mastery.

t: Why Your Class Must Be Hard
q: Men wanted for hazardous journey. Low wages, bitter cold, long hours of complete darkness. Safe return doubtful. Honour and recognition in event of success.
We all want to be part of something bigger than ourselves. It’s a longing of human nature the best teachers, coaches, and business leaders use to motivate and inspire.
It makes school ordinary. And kids don’t like ordinary. None of us do. It inspires nothing. It makes even the idea of it exhausting. Unremarkable, mediocre, boring, easy, lazy, slow, soul crushing.
The truth is, you should never lower standards, for any reason. You should never give unlimited time for assignments, dumb down your curriculum, or pass along students unearned.

It provides meaning and self worth. It produces pride and confidence and discipline. It gives them something they’re unlikely getting anywhere else: The feeling of belonging to something remarkable and knowing that they have a higher purpose .

t: Learning Lesson 7: Bad Learning Strategies Are Popular
q: Students often prefer the least effective study strategies for long-term learning. Let's get it down, and then let's talk about strategies that work and strategies that don't.
Now notice a commonality between the three of these: all of them are kind of passive. Remember how fired up I got yesterday talking about being aggressive? That's the opposite of passive.
The trouble, of course, is that being familiar with your notes doesn't mean that you've learned the course material. You've just built some vague pictures in your mind of what the notes look like.
The solutions, then are to basically get AGGRESSIVE with understanding what the heck you're supposed to learn and getting that information organized in your mind.

As you're studying, focus on creating meaning — on understanding what you're trying to learn about. Organize information into meaningful chunks. Elaborate on the information you're learning — try to make connections between it and other things you know.

t: Learning Lesson 6: Multitasking is popular, but it doesn't work
q: Pitfall #1: Multitasking and distractions GREATLY reduce learning. Modern humans insanely underestimate the degree to which distractions harm their learning.
I want you to start thinking about learning a little more like an athlete, a little more like a gamer, a little more like someone who WANTS something, okay? Because listen — you DO want to learn.
And I remember one day my coach saying for the hundredth time, "Dave — be aggressive. Get in there. Go for it." And for whatever reason, that day it clicked.

When you're studying, just study. Set a timer for 25 minutes and for that 25 minutes you look at no other tabs, you chuck that phone right out the door, you put in some earbuds and you Just. Focus. On. Learning.
I've literally had students who study in the closet because it's the best hideout they can get in their living arrangement.

t: Why Your New Classroom Management Plan Isn't Working
q: Not five minutes after teaching your plan, your students are right back at it; misbehaving as if nothing has changed. So what happened?
When through several months of the school year you show yourself to be one person, your students won’t believe you when you all of a sudden claim to be someone else.
However, your students can sense it. They feel it in their bones when you’re less than 100 percent committed. Show any weakness—tone of voice, posture, non-verbal expression—and they’ll know it.

You were lightening the shock of change . You were saying the right things but with caveats and qualifiers. You were warming them up to the idea of full accountability instead of sticking your flag in the ground.

You can be nervous and fumble over your words. You can be the worst communicator of all time and do all three of the above and then some. And although it may take longer, if you’re consistent, you’ll get there.

The truth is, they want discipline. They want high standards. They want to be part of something special. They crave it deep inside, beyond their awareness. It doesn’t matter who they are or where you work.
